questions.stem: Six hours after a long leg cast was applied for a tibial fracture, a 22-year-old client rates pain 9 out of 10 despite IV morphine 30 minutes ago. The pain gets worse when the nurse gently moves the toes. The pedal pulse is still present. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Compartment syndrome
Expected fracture pain
Fat embolism syndrome
Acute osteomyelitis

rationale.correct: Compartment syndrome: severe pain unrelieved by opioids and pain with passive stretch come early; pallor and pulselessness are late.

perOption.a: Pain out of proportion to the injury and pain on passive stretch are the earliest signs; pulses are lost late.
perOption.b: Expected pain eases with analgesics and is not worsened by moving the toes.
perOption.c: Fat embolism causes respiratory and neurological signs.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse suspects compartment syndrome in a client with a casted forearm fracture. The fingers are swollen and pale, and the client says the hand feels "tight and tingly." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Notify the provider now and keep the arm level with the heart
Raise the arm on pillows well above the level of the client's heart
Apply ice packs around the cast and reassess in 2 hours
Give another dose of the prescribed IV opioid

rationale.correct: Compartment syndrome: notify the provider at once, keep the limb at heart level, loosen dressings and prepare for fasciotomy.

perOption.a: Prompt notification allows the cast to be split or a fasciotomy; raising the arm above the heart further reduces flow.
perOption.b: Raising it above the heart can reduce arterial flow further.
perOption.c: Delay can lead to permanent damage.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: Two days after a femur fracture from a motorcycle crash, a 24-year-old client suddenly becomes confused and short of breath, with an SpO2 of 86% and a temperature of 38.4 °C. The nurse notes tiny red spots across the chest and armpits. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Fat embolism syndrome
Hospital-acquired pneumonia
Anxiety about the injury
Compartment syndrome

rationale.correct: Fat embolism usually appears 24 to 72 hours after a long bone fracture: hypoxemia, confusion and petechiae.

perOption.a: Fat droplets from a long bone fracture cause respiratory distress, confusion and petechiae.
perOption.b: Pneumonia develops more gradually and does not cause petechiae.
perOption.c: This does not explain the hypoxemia or petechiae.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is doing hourly neurovascular checks on a client with a newly casted right forearm. Which assessments should be included? Select all that apply.

options.text: Pain level and its response to medication
Color of the fingers
Radial pulse below the cast
Sensation in the fingers
Bowel sounds in all four quadrants
Blood pressure in the casted arm

rationale.correct: Check the 6 Ps: pain, pallor, pulse, paresthesia, paralysis and poikilothermia (temperature).

perOption.a: Increasing pain can signal ischemia.
perOption.b: Pallor or cyanosis suggests poor perfusion.
perOption.c: Weak or absent pulses suggest arterial compromise.
perOption.d: Numbness or tingling suggests nerve compression.
perOption.e: These are not part of a neurovascular check.
perOption.f: A cuff is not placed on the casted limb.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with a new fiberglass cast on the lower leg is going home with a parent. Which statement shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "We'll keep the leg up on pillows for the first day or two."
"A straightened coat hanger will help with itching under it."
"We'll call if the toes feel numb or look pale or blue."
"We'll cover the cast with a plastic bag whenever it's bath time."

rationale.correct: Cast care: elevate, keep it dry, put nothing inside, and report neurovascular changes.

perOption.a: Elevation reduces swelling.
perOption.b: Objects can break the skin and cause infection.
perOption.d: Keeping the cast dry protects the skin.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 82-year-old client with a hip fracture awaiting surgery is in Buck's skin traction. Which observation by the nurse requires intervention?

options.text: The weights hang freely off the end of the bed
The weights are resting on the floor
The heel of the affected leg is off the bed
The rope runs through the groove of the pulley

rationale.correct: Traction: the weights hang freely, the ropes run in the pulleys and the client stays aligned.

perOption.a: This is correct.
perOption.b: Weights on the floor provide no traction.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is doing pin care for a client in skeletal traction for a femur fracture. Which finding at a pin site should the nurse report to the provider?

options.text: Thick yellow drainage with spreading redness
A small amount of clear, watery drainage
A thin crust where the pin enters the skin
Mild tenderness on the first day after insertion

rationale.correct: Pin care: clean per protocol and report purulent drainage, spreading redness or fever.

perOption.a: This suggests infection, which can lead to osteomyelitis.
perOption.b: Serous drainage is expected.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: An 84-year-old client fell at home and cannot stand. The client reports pain in the right groin. Which finding suggests a hip fracture?

options.text: The right leg is shorter and turned outward
The right leg is longer and turned inward
There is bruising over the right knee only
The right hip moves fully without pain

rationale.correct: Hip fracture: shortening, external rotation and groin or hip pain.

perOption.a: These are classic signs of a hip fracture.
perOption.b: This is not typical.
perOption.c: This does not indicate a hip fracture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old client is going home 2 days after a total hip replacement done through a posterior approach. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll use the raised toilet seat that was delivered."
"I'll keep the wedge pillow between my legs in bed."
"I'll cross my legs at the ankles when I sit."
"I'll use the grabber instead of bending to the floor."

rationale.correct: Posterior hip precautions: no flexion beyond 90 degrees, no crossing the legs and no turning the leg inward.

perOption.a: This avoids bending the hip more than 90 degrees.
perOption.b: This keeps the hip abducted.
perOption.c: Crossing the legs can dislocate the hip.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Teach hip precautions after hip replacement.

questions.stem: One day after a total hip replacement, a client turns in bed without help and suddenly reports severe pain in the operative hip. The operative leg now looks shorter and is rotated inward. The pedal pulse is present, and the foot is warm. Which complication does the nurse suspect?

options.text: Dislocation of the hip prosthesis
Expected incisional pain
Deep vein thrombosis
Surgical site infection

rationale.correct: Report a suspected dislocation immediately and keep the leg still.

perOption.a: Sudden pain with shortening and rotation after a turn suggests dislocation.
perOption.b: A sudden change in leg position is not expected.
perOption.c: DVT causes calf swelling and pain, not shortening.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old client with a body mass index of 34 is 1 day after a total knee replacement. Which plan best reduces the risk of deep vein thrombosis?

options.text: Early walking, the prescribed anticoagulant and compression devices
A pillow under the knee to keep the new joint comfortable and raised up
Bed rest for a week so that the new joint can heal fully
Limiting fluids to reduce swelling around the new knee

rationale.correct: After joint replacement: anticoagulation, mechanical compression, early mobility and hydration.

perOption.a: Mobility and prophylaxis reduce venous stasis.
perOption.b: This can cause a flexion contracture and does not prevent DVT.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is checking how a client with a sprained ankle uses axillary crutches before discharge. Which observation requires the nurse to correct the client?

options.text: The client leans on the underarm pads to rest
There are 2 to 3 finger widths between the armpit and the pad
The elbows bend about 30 degrees on the hand grips
The crutch tips are about 15 cm to the side of each foot

rationale.correct: Crutches: weight on the hands, a 2 to 3 finger gap at the armpit and elbows bent 20 to 30 degrees.

perOption.a: Pressure on the armpits can damage the brachial plexus; weight goes on the hands.
perOption.b: This is the correct fit.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a right ankle fracture who must not bear weight on that leg is learning to go up stairs with crutches. Which instruction is correct?

options.text: "Step up with your left leg, then bring the crutches and right leg."
"Step up with your right leg first, then bring up the crutches."
"Put the crutches on the step above first, then step up with both legs."
"Hold the rail and hop up the stairs without the crutches."

rationale.correct: Stairs: up with the good leg; down with the crutches and the injured leg.

perOption.a: "Up with the good": the strong leg leads going up.
perOption.b: The injured leg cannot bear the lift.
perOption.c: The good leg leads going up.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with weakness of the left leg after a stroke is learning to walk with a single-point cane. How should the client use the cane?

options.text: In the right hand, moving it forward with the left leg
In the left hand, moving it forward with the left leg
In the right hand, moving it forward with the right leg
In either hand, placed well out in front of the body

rationale.correct: Cane: held on the strong side and moved forward with the weak leg.

perOption.a: The cane on the strong side supports the weak leg.
perOption.b: The cane goes on the strong side.
perOption.c: The cane moves with the weak leg.
perOption.d: It is held about 15 cm to the side, close to the body.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with a weak right leg after a knee replacement is learning to use a standard walker. Place the steps in order, from first to last.

items.text: Step forward with the weak (right) leg
Step forward with the strong (left) leg
Lift the walker and move it forward about one step's length

rationale.correct: Walker: move the walker, then the weak leg, then the strong leg.

perOption.a: The walker moves first to provide a base of support.
perOption.b: The weak leg moves into the walker while the arms support the weight.

references: Fundamentals of nursing texts (e.g. Potter & Perry)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 52-year-old postmenopausal woman who smokes 10 cigarettes a day and drinks several colas daily asks how to protect her bones. Which advice is best?

options.text: Get enough calcium and vitamin D, and do weight-bearing exercise
Switch from cola to diet cola and keep the same amount
Avoid exercise so that the bones are not put under any extra stress
Cut down to five cigarettes a day to protect the bones

rationale.correct: Osteoporosis prevention: calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, no smoking, limited alcohol and fall prevention.

perOption.a: These build and maintain bone mass.
perOption.b: Cola, diet or not, may reduce bone density.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with osteoporosis is starting alendronate 70 mg once a week. Which statement by the client shows correct understanding?

options.text: "I'll take it on waking with plain water and stay upright for 30 minutes."
"I'll take it with my breakfast and my morning coffee so that I remember it."
"I'll take it at bedtime and lie down right afterward to sleep."
"I'll take it with my calcium tablet so they work together."

rationale.correct: Bisphosphonates: empty stomach, plain water, upright for 30 minutes, and no other food or drugs for 30 minutes.

perOption.a: This prevents esophageal irritation and allows absorption.
perOption.b: Food and drinks other than water reduce absorption.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is assessing two clinic clients with joint pain, one with osteoarthritis and one with rheumatoid arthritis. For each finding, choose the condition it is more typical of.

rows.text: Morning stiffness lasting more than 1 hour
Bony nodes at the finger joints nearest the nails
The same joints affected on both sides of the body
Joint pain that worsens with use and eases with rest
Fatigue, low-grade fever and weight loss

rationale.correct: OA: degenerative, worse with use, Heberden nodes. RA: autoimmune, symmetric, long morning stiffness and systemic symptoms.

perOption.r1:c1: OA stiffness usually lasts under 30 minutes.
perOption.r1:c2: Prolonged morning stiffness is typical of RA.
perOption.r2:c1: Heberden nodes are typical of OA.
perOption.r2:c2: RA affects the knuckles and wrists rather than causing these nodes.
perOption.r4:c1: Wear-and-tear pain is typical of OA.
perOption.r4:c2: RA pain is often worse after rest.
perOption.r5:c1: OA does not cause systemic symptoms.
perOption.r5:c2: RA is a systemic autoimmune disease.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Tell osteoarthritis apart from rheumatoid arthritis.

questions.stem: A 58-year-old client with gout who had a flare in the big toe last month is choosing meals from a menu. Which choice shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: Low-fat yogurt with fresh fruit
Fried liver with onions and a beer
A bowl of cherries as a snack
A large glass of water with each meal

rationale.correct: Gout: limit purines (organ meats, shellfish), alcohol (especially beer) and fructose, and drink plenty of fluids.

perOption.a: Low-fat dairy may lower uric acid.
perOption.b: Organ meats and beer are high in purines and raise uric acid.
perOption.d: Fluids help the kidneys excrete uric acid.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A client with recurrent gout attacks and a uric acid of 9.4 mg/dL is starting allopurinol daily. The client also has colchicine at home. Which statement by the client shows a need for more teaching?

options.text: "I'll take the allopurinol every day, even when my joints feel fine."
"I'll take extra allopurinol to stop the pain if my toe flares up."
"I'll drink plenty of water every day while I'm on it."
"I'll call right away if I notice a rash or blisters."

rationale.correct: Allopurinol prevents gout by lowering uric acid; it does not treat acute flares.

perOption.a: Allopurinol is a long-term preventive drug.
perOption.b: Allopurinol does not treat acute attacks; colchicine, NSAIDs or steroids do.
perOption.d: A rash can signal a serious reaction.

references: Nursing pharmacology texts (e.g. Lehne; McCuistion) and the drug's prescribing information
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 66-year-old client with peripheral arterial disease had an above-the-knee amputation 2 days ago and spends most of the day sitting up in a chair. Which intervention helps prevent a hip flexion contracture?

options.text: Lying prone for periods several times a day
A pillow under the residual limb while in bed
Sitting in the chair for longer each day
The head of the bed raised most of the day

rationale.correct: After amputation: prone positioning, no pillows under the limb after 24 hours and limited sitting.

perOption.a: Lying face down stretches the hip flexors.
perOption.b: After the first 24 hours, this promotes a hip flexion contracture.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A week after a below-the-knee amputation, a client says, "My missing foot is burning and cramping. Am I going crazy?" What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Phantom limb pain is real, and it can be treated."
"That isn't possible, because your foot has been removed."
"It's your mind playing tricks on you, so try to ignore it."
"This kind of pain usually lasts for the rest of your life."

rationale.correct: Phantom limb pain is real; it may be treated with medications, mirror therapy and other approaches.

perOption.a: Phantom pain comes from nerve signals and responds to treatment.
perOption.b: This dismisses a real experience.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching a client to wrap a below-the-knee residual limb with an elastic bandage before a prosthesis is fitted. Which technique is correct?

options.text: A figure-eight pattern, firmest at the end of the limb
Circular turns, tightest just below the knee
Loose turns with no overlap, for comfort
Wrapping it only at night while the client sleeps, then removing it

rationale.correct: Residual limb wrapping: a figure-eight pattern, distal to proximal, firmest at the end.

perOption.a: This shapes the limb into a cone for a prosthesis.
perOption.b: This restricts blood flow.
perOption.c: This will not shape the limb.
perOption.d: Wrapping is usually continuous and redone several times a day.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.

questions.stem: A 46-year-old data entry clerk reports numbness at night in the thumb, index and middle fingers. When the client holds both wrists fully flexed for 60 seconds, the numbness returns. Which condition does this suggest?

options.text: Carpal tunnel syndrome
Gouty arthritis
Rheumatoid arthritis
Raynaud phenomenon

rationale.correct: Carpal tunnel syndrome: positive Phalen and Tinel signs; wrist splints and ergonomic changes help.

perOption.a: A positive Phalen test suggests median nerve compression.
perOption.b: Gout causes a hot, swollen joint.
perOption.c: This is not what the Phalen test detects.
perOption.d: This involves color changes with cold.

references: Medical-surgical nursing texts (e.g. Lewis; Ignatavicius)
Rewritten to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 19 November 2026.
